title: Design Add And Search Words Data Structure
statement: Build a word store with addWord(word) and search(pattern). A pattern is made of lowercase letters and dots, and a dot stands for any single letter. search returns true when some stored word has the same length as the pattern and matches it letter by letter.

example.caption: Stored: bad, dad, mad, dot. The pattern d.t starts with d, then the dot tries a and o. Only the o branch can end in t.

output.label: search(d.t) is true through d, o, t

idea.sentence: A plain letter has one way down the trie, but a dot branches into every child, so the search becomes a depth-first search that tries each branch and backs up on failure.

jargon.plain: A symbol that matches many things. Here a dot matches any one letter.
Go as deep as you can down one branch. If it fails, back up one step and try the next branch.
A tree where each edge is one letter and shared prefixes are stored once.

watch.inputHint: Two arguments: the operation names, then their arguments, e.g. ["WordDictionary","addWord","search"], [[],["bad"],["b.d"]]

compare.bruteLabel: Compare the pattern with every stored word
compare.unit: steps per search. With no dots a trie search is only L steps, which is far less

rows.name: List of words
rows.note: Every search compares against every word of the same length.

rows.name: Trie, no dots
rows.note: One path down, one node per letter.

rows.name: Trie, with dots
rows.note: Each dot fans out. Worst case, a pattern of only dots visits every node up to depth L.

fast.takeaway: The trie helps most when letters are known: a wrong letter cuts a whole branch at once. Dots give that back, so only dots cost a fan-out.

stages.title: Empty root
stages.note: Make one empty root node for the empty prefix.

stages.title: addWord
stages.note: Walk down the word, reusing or creating a child per letter, then set the end flag on the last node.

stages.title: Plain letter
stages.note: Look up the one child with that letter. If it is missing, this branch fails.

stages.title: Dot: try every child
stages.note: Recurse into each child in turn with the next letter. Return true as soon as one branch works.

stages.title: Pattern used up
stages.note: When all letters are consumed, succeed only if this node ends a stored word.

edges.title: Empty dictionary
edges.why: A dot needs at least one child to try. The root has none, so the loop runs zero times.

edges.title: Pattern longer than the word
edges.why: After a there are no children, so the second dot has nothing to match. A dot never matches nothing.

edges.title: Pattern is a prefix
edges.why: All letters match, but the node is not a word end. The end flag is the last check.

edges.title: All dots
edges.why: The first branch already works, so the search stops there and does not touch the others.

gotchas.text: A dot must match exactly one letter. A shorter or longer stored word never matches, which is why the end flag is checked only when the pattern is used up.
Do not return false after the first failed child. Return false only after the loop has tried all children.
A plain object as the children map breaks on keys such as "constructor" or "__proto__". Use a Map, which also gives you for...of over the children for the dot case.
A map field is nil until you make it, and writing to a nil map panics. Create children together with the node.
Go map iteration order is random, so the dot branches are tried in a different order each run. The boolean answer is the same, only the work done may differ.

recap.key: A letter follows one child. A dot recurses into all children and succeeds if any branch does.
recap.complexity: addWord O(L). search O(L) without dots, up to O(nodes) with. Space O(letters).
moves: addWord: insert into a trie and flag the last node
Plain letter: follow the single child or fail
Dot: try every child, return true on the first success
Pattern used up: succeed only on a word-end node
